title: Database Engine Engineering Database — Overview and definition
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Indexes, query planners, transaction systems, storage engines, and benchmark results. The Database Engine Engineering Database documents how databases themselves are built: index structures that make lookups fast, query planners that choose execution strategies, transaction systems that keep data consistent, storage engines that persist it, and benchmarks that measure the result. Anyone building or choosing a database needs this machinery visible — the record format exposes the engineering trade-offs instead of hiding them behind marketing.

title: Database Engine Engineering Database — Knowledge: technical reference
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Indexes: B-tree (O(log n) point/range, good for mixed workloads); LSM-tree (memtable + SSTables, great writes, compaction reads cost); hash (O(1) point lookups, no ranges); bitmap (low-cardinality analytics). Query planning: parse -> logical plan -> cost-based optimization (join order by selectivity estimates, index selection) -> physical plan; EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan. Transactions: ACID; isolation levels (read-uncommitted < read-committed < repeatable-read < serializable); MVCC keeps old row versions for readers; WAL (write-ahead log) enables crash recovery: redo committed, undo uncommitted. Storage: pages (4-16KB), slotted pages for variable rows, compression trade-offs (CPU vs I/O). Benchmarks: state workload (YCSB-style mix), dataset size, cache state, and config — without these, numbers are meaningless.

title: Database Engine Engineering Database — Verification: tests and limitations
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Tests: cost-math test (complexity claims match the structures); anomaly test (each isolation level exhibits exactly its documented anomalies); benchmark test (records missing config are rejected); determinism test. Limitations: cost models are approximate; real planners use statistics the demos simplify; benchmark numbers are as-reported with config. Every benchmark record is config-complete or flagged incomplete.
